How much does motorcycle tire replacement cost?

One new tire, mounted and balanced — what it costs, and what moves the price:

$150–$300

Tire $100–$400 · mounting $20–$50 · rears wear ~2x faster than fronts

Bay Area: no published metro-specific figure found — the national range is the honest reference.

Why quotes run $120 to $450

Tire type
Sport tires average $150–$250, up to $400 for premium. Budget brands run $100–$150 — less grip, shorter life.
Mounting
$20–$50 per tire at a shop; more if they pull the wheel off the bike. Bring the loose wheel and pay the least.
Front vs. rear
Rears wear roughly twice as fast. Budget for two rears per front — and never mix a dead rear with a fresh front and call it fine.
Size
Bigger, wider, and oddball sizes cost more. Standard sportbike sizes have the most competition and the best prices.
Premium vs. budget

What the extra money buys

Budget
$100–$150

Fine for commuting and easy miles. Harder compounds last longer but give up grip — know what you're trading.

Premium
$200–$400

Better grip, better feel, often better mileage than you'd expect. On a motorcycle, tires are not where you economize.

Bottom line: your contact patches are two palm-sized ovals. Buy the best tire you can justify — it's the cheapest safety upgrade on the bike.

Common questions

How long do motorcycle tires last?

5,000–15,000 miles depending on compound and riding style. Soft sport rubber can be done in one aggressive season.

How do I know it's time?

Tread wear bars flush with the tread, a squared-off profile, or any cracking. Check the date code too — replace at five years regardless of tread.

Can I mount it myself?

With tire irons, patience, and a balancer, yes. Most riders pay the $20–$50 — pinched tubes and scratched rims are the usual tuition.

Should I replace both at once?

Only if both are due. Rears die twice as fast — replacing a good front with the rear is spending money for symmetry.

Every bike prices differently.

The range above is a national average. Your price depends on the tire, the size, and who mounts it. Take a photo of your tire's sidewall in Brightglow for an estimate on the actual bike.
